short_definition: A password manager is an app that generates, stores and auto-fills strong, unique passwords for each of your accounts in an encrypted vault, unlocked with one master password or device authentication.
explanation: A password manager lets you use a different strong password for every account while only remembering one. It creates long random passwords, stores them encrypted, syncs them across your devices and fills them in on the correct websites. Autofill also helps you spot phishing, because the manager won't fill your details on a fake site whose address doesn't match. Options include standalone apps and the managers built into browsers and operating systems. Many can also store passkeys and two-factor codes. Features and pricing vary, so confirm them on the vendor's website.

Reusing passwords is dangerous because a breach at one site lets attackers try the same email and password on other sites, a technique called credential stuffing. With unique passwords, a breach at one site exposes only that one account.

The trade-off is that all your secrets are kept in one place. The master password must be strong and unique, and the password manager account should have two-factor authentication turned on. Depending on the provider's recovery options, forgetting the master password can mean losing access to the vault. Choose a reputable provider, set up recovery and emergency access, and keep the app updated.
example: Illustrative example: You have 60 online accounts and use 3 variations of the same password across all of them. You install a password manager. You start with your 10 most important accounts (email, bank, phone carrier and work), give each a unique 20-character random password and turn on 2FA. If a shopping site is breached later, only that one account's password is exposed.
common_mistake: Protecting the password manager with a weak or reused master password, or not turning on two-factor authentication for the password manager itself.
title: Password Manager
